samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Lee P. Riggin was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Your name and -- your full name and then just, you know, from Laurel, Delaware, and then after that, then just tell me basically from birth, I was born in such and such a time. I was born up in Pennsylvania and my mother and father were in the whatever.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And then just tell me the story leading up to actually Pearl Harbor Day. You remember Pearl Harbor Day, where you were?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Just sort of lead me in the story from starting out with your name, Laurel, Delaware, and then where you were born, how you were raised and all that.

sp.speaker: Videographer
sp.p: TJ, this, today, since you are sitting further away and we are in a small space here --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: My hands. I can't be animated.

sp.speaker: Videographer
sp.p: Use the left hand to be animated.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: My name is Lee Riggin, and I was born in Clearfield, Pennsylvania, August 21st, 1924. My family lived in Clearfield for about two years, but they were from Laurel for the last couple hundred years. Father worked there in a coal mine for about two years, and of course that's where I was born. We moved back to Laurel in 1926, and I went to school, graduated from Laurel High School in 1943. And in 19 -- December the 7th, 1941, I worked at the theater here in town as the door man, and I was going to the theater that afternoon to do some work, turn up the seats or something like that, and that's when I heard about Pearl Harbor. And of course it was a shock, because probably I didn't even know where Pearl Harbor was, but I knew it was a bad time for the United States. I think we were probably going to wind up in the war. I had a cousin killed at Pearl Harbor, by the way. He was on the Destroyer Shaw, and he was the first Delawarian killed in WWII, being at Pearl Harbor. He lived in Millsboro.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Tell me his full name, and 'cause he's -- I've got -- we've got newspaper articles about him. There was two of them, I think, that were killed in Pearl Harbor, the first casualties.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: At Pearl Harbor there were two?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I think so. I think he was the first one.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Well, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Tell me his name. Do you have -- do you know know his name?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: All I can think of is Junior. Penule. (Phonetic) I can't think of his first name. His last name is Penule, and he's Junior, Junior Penule.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You want to stop the roll for just a second? (Off-the-record discussion) THE WITNESS: We all called him -- INTERVIEW:

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Two guys were killed on the Shaw. He was the first one that was killed.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: He was the Bosun's mate.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: He was originally in the 261st. In 1936 or '37 he went in, which was the National Guard.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And then in January of '41 -- January of '41, went in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Uh-huh. Yeah. That's him, George

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. We're rolling again.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So tell me about Pearl Harbor and then getting us where the cousin was killed at Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Okay. Pearl Harbor was, of course, December the 7th, '41, and I heard about it on my way to the theater Sunday afternoon, where I was going to do a little house cleaning. And of course I was shocked like everybody else. And had a personal relationship with the day, because my cousin, George

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Penule, was on the USS Shaw, and was the first Delawarian killed at Pearl Harbor. In 1943 I graduated from Laurel High on June the 8th, and already I got my orders on July the 8th. I left to go to Fort Dix and was processed through there and sent to Miami Beach. I was in the United States Air Corps, and we spent two months taking basic training, stayed in hotels on beach front. I did PT on the same. Went swimming in the afternoon, and at that point I didn't even know the war was on. That was good duty. But that finished at the end of the summer, and I had taken some courses, bookkeeping and typing and accounting courses in school, in high school, and I guess that showed up in my Army record, so I was sent to North Dakota Agricultural College in Fargo, North Dakota, to take an eight-week Army administration school course. After I finished that in January of '44, I was sent back to Florida, to MacDill Air Force Base, and landed another nice job there. I was the armament and ordinance clerk for a Major Clemens for a B17 bomb group. I had my own office. I had my own transportation back and forth to the barracks. I went to work at eight or nine o'clock in the morning, finished at 4:00 in the afternoon and, again, I didn't know the war was on. It was -- it was good duty. That lasted, let's see, this is '44, that lasted through '44, and by that time in Europe, the bulge had started, the Germans had broke through in December, and the Army had stated that people in my category who were doing clerking duties were needed in Europe, so they transferred thousands, tens of thousands of people like myself to various infantry training schools around the country. I was sent to Camp Gordon, Georgia, and -- in December of '44, and received eight weeks of what they -- called Army Infantry Transition Training School. They were going to teach me how to be an infantryman. I lost my rank. I was a corporal. I lost my rank, which of course so did everyone else. There were people who were staff sergeants and tech sergeants who were broke down to private and got the infantry training. So we spent eight weeks there with a complete infantry training to learn how to kill Germans. Then we were sent to -- people that I was with were sent to Europe. We had left Fort Dix and then the Port of New York sometime in early March of '45, and arrived in France, oh, 10 or 12 days later, and were sent to replacement depot, and I was assigned to the 7th Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, which happened to be commanded by another Delawarian, a Major John R. Michael Daniel. He met several of us replacements at the replacement depot the second day we were there and told us how happy he was to see us and what we could expect as part of the 3rd Infantry Division. From there I was assigned to a company and went into combat just as we crossed the Rhine and spent the rest of the next six weeks in combat through Germany. We captured several small towns. We were at combat in several large towns, Augsburg, Munich, and a couple of more. An interesting thing, I suppose I didn't realize it at the time that it was that much interest, but it was a real surprise. On one of the days, we had just captured a small town in Central Germany, and we were out on the street. Guys were just laying around doing -- smoking or whatever, you know. Civilians would come out of the house, and there was a bomb, a couple of bombs hit. Well, we had been under artillery fire before, and you hear them coming, most of the time. You at least here the report or the shell coming, but we heard nothing until the bomb exploded. And our platoon leader, a lieutenant and a couple of GIs and about four civilians, were killed. Come to find out later, it was a jet plane. It was one of the very, very few German jet planes that they had got into combat. It had got combat ready and were dropping bombs. We had some tanks in town, so I'm pretty sure that's what they were after is to get the tanks. They didn't, but they killed three GIs and some of their own people, the German civilians. I guess of other interest would be the fact that our division, our regiment, battle patrol from our regiment was the first one into Berchtesgaden at the end of the war, about the 5th of May. It was a prize that everyone wanted to be the first one there, and actually it wasn't assigned to the 3rd Division, it was assigned to the 101st Airborne Division or the Second Armored French Division. But our commanding general saw an opportunity to be there first, because there was only two bridges leading into town that anybody had -- nobody had occupied them yet. So he sent a battle patrol out with orders to a Lt. Nathan White to hold these bridges with his platoon until he gave orders to let somebody come over. He allowed nobody except the 7th Regiment people to come in through Berchtesgaden. Several hundred of the troops, myself included, were able to cross that bridge and be the first one into Berchtesgaden and on up to Hitler's home. The commanding general of the second French Army Division was a General McClair, and he was quite famous. And he came up and ordered the American, the Lt. White, to allow him to cross the bridge. Lt. White called back to the general, our general, Daniel, and asked him about orders. He said hold them there a little while longer, which he did, but I guess the German -- the French general just went ballistic, to be held up by an ally and told he couldn't cross the bridge, but the lieutenant had his orders, so he kept him there. 101st Airborne Division came over later, and in just a couple of days the 7th Regiment and the 3rd Division left and went into Salzburg, and we occupied Salzburg for about two months. But we were the first outfit into -- Obersalzburg, which is the name of the compound, was Hitler's home. I have some souvenirs from there, a piece of tile from the bathroom at Hitler's home, a piece of granite from the fireplace in Hitler's home, and a piece of tile from Martin Bohrman's swimming pool, which was in the compound, and also a gravy boat from the guest house in Obersalzburg. We left --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Hold on a second. Tell me about that a little more. How did you find it when you got there? I mean, how did -- was it bombed? Was it shelled? Was it rubble? What was going on there?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: The Hitler's home itself was not in too bad shape. Windows had been blown out, of course. We weren't allowed on the second floor because it had taken some bombs and the roof had collapsed, but the entire second floor of the basement and the patio outside was all open, so we could go into any part of that we wanted to. Most of the rest of the compound was pretty well destroyed. Martin Bohrman's home was destroyed, Herman Gehrig's home was destroyed, the SS barracks were all destroyed, but fortunately most of Hitler's home was still accessible. You could go in most any part of it except the second floor.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did you have any resistance going into the town?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: No. They had all given up. It was no fire fights at all.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What were you doing with the prisoners? Were you doing anything with the prisoners, then, or --

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Well, at that time, the combat troops, like myself, just passing by. They had laid down their arms and we just passed them by. As a matter of fact, I'll back up a little bit. On the way into Berchtesgarden we were going down -- we were on trucks. We were no longer on foot, because everything was moving fast. It's about the 1st, 2nd, 3rd of May, something like that. And we were on trucks going down the autobahn as fast as the trucks could go. And in the center of the autobahn, between the two lanes, there were thousands and thousands and thousands of German troops just waiting there for somebody to tell them what to do. We passed airports with the planes still out in the field, and we thought this is nice, except that I wondered what are they going to do after we get past them, you know. Are they going to change their mind, decide they're going to fight again. They didn't, but it was kind of eerie to go past all these troops who were just waiting for somebody to tell them what to do. But the front line troops, combat troops, we did not bother with them, because there was too many. We -- the troops came behind us and set up troop or prison compounds. Most of the time they just set them up for several days in fields and put wires around them, but they -- the fight was all out of them. They were very pleased for this thing to be over. So......

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So you're in Salzburg.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: We went to Salzburg and we occupied Salzburg for a couple of months, and the European war was still on. The Pacific war was still on and, of course, we were sweating out then what's going to happen to us, because we already knew some outfits were going to be sent to the Pacific. Finally we got the word that we were going to be on occupation in Germany, so we would not be going to the Pacific theater, and that was good news.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What was it, if you could tell me, what happened in Italy and that fall way first, or how did that happen when -- Mussolini and stuff? Was that way before?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: That was well before all this action took place.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: That was like like during France and the occupation of France and Paris and --

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Oh, yeah. He gave up.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: The Germans fought on, but the Italians had gave up.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How about in North Africa, how did that -- did that just come to a stop? Was that still going on or was that already over?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: No, that had happened long before that. The 3rd Infantry Division went into North Africa in November of '42 and they fought through there, through North Africa into Sicily and Italy, so that all ended in '43. North Africa was all over. They finished. They'd occupied North Africa, they'd occupied Sicily, they went into Italy, and that was pretty much over about '45.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So the big push after that was actually the bulge?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Yeah. The Central Europe.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Bulge and then Germany?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Yeah. We didn't get into the bulge, thank heavens, in Southern Germany, 'cause that must have been a very difficult time. I have been to Bastone in one of my trips to -- back to Europe. Need to pay my respects to the people that were there, because they had a tough time. So we were warring in an occupation zone right next to the Russians in Central Germany. We were in a small -- my regiment, 7th Regiment was headquartered in a town called Hersfeld, and we were only about five miles from the Russian border, and the Germans were glad to see us there, German civilians were glad to see us there, because they were deathly afraid of the Russians.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How did you guys get along with the Russians?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: We got along fine. We got along great with them. They might get drunk once in a while and come across the border and shoot up the German towns, scare the hell out of the German civilians, but we'd chase them back, tell them to go on back. We had no problems. I got a leave in November of '45, I guess it was, to go to Berlin. At -- it was maybe 15 or 20 of us, and we met several Russians, and they were -- Russian combat troops were still there. We got along fine with them. We traded cigarettes and watches and that kind of thing, you know, bartered with them. I tried my best to get one of the red stars off their helmet, but I couldn't get it. They wouldn't part with it. It was funny, we didn't know -- they didn't know English, we didn't know Russian, but we talked in German. What German they had picked up, what German we had picked up, we managed with it. But we got along fine. As a matter of fact, they got along so fine that it wasn't very long after that they sent all the Russian combat troops back home. They sent new ones to occupy the area with orders not to get along so well with the Americans, so we heard.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So how long did you stay over in Europe?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: I stayed in Army of Occupation in the first spell, until March of '46. And by that time, of course, the things were pretty well settled down over there. We had very little, if any, trouble with the German civilians. And I was sent home, got home in April of '46 and was discharged at Fort Dix and came home.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now you get home, are -- were you married yet, or weren't you married yet?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: I was married.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Tell me about that. Tell me how -- tell me when you got married and, you know, it was during the war, and tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: I got married, as a matter of fact, just before I went overseas. We had been engaged. It was a high school girl friend, sweetheart, and we were engaged before I went in the service, and we married while I was in the service and before I went overseas. And looking back on it, it was kind of a ridiculous thing to do, but who knows when you're 19 years old, you know, and you're in love. We decided that we wanted to get married before I went overseas and I knew I was going into combat. If my son had wanted to do the same thing, I would have said you lost your mind, which is of course is what they told us. But it all worked out. We got back safely, and never sorry that we did it, that we got married before I went over.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So you got discharged, you came back to -- coming home, then what did you do?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Came back to Laurel and worked in the Marlboro Package Company (phonetic), which is just down the hill here, as paymaster for about two years. Then I worked -- went to work for Metropolitan Life Insurance Company. I spent 20 years with them. And then I went to work for Kiwanis International and spent 21 years with them. Stayed right here in Laurel during the whole time, and still live here now. As a matter of fact, today is my 60th wedding anniversary. 60 years we've been married.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Congratulations.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: This very day.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Congratulations.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Any children, or --

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Two children. We have a boy and a girl. Boy who is a Marine Corps veteran himself, was in Vietnam, and a daughter who -- he lives in Petersburg, and a daughter who works in Wilmington, or Dover, now, for Wilmington Trust. And three grandchildren and three great grandchildren and another one on the way. Be here in April.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Nice.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What would you -- what would you want future generations, you know, to take out of World War II? What would your comment be about World War II to future generations?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Never let it happen again, which means I support what they did in Iraq. You can't let these bullies out of their boxes. We unfortunately let Hitler out of his box in the '30s and didn't stop him, and we could have stopped him. Anybody could have stopped him in the '30s. They didn't do it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How do you see this generation right now as opposed to you guys, when you were growing up?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: You mean the 20 and 30 year olds, or --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: A little younger than that, maybe, in the 20 to 30, that whole generation.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Yeah. I'm very proud of them. I think they're a great generation. I have a grandson who's in the U.S. Navy, stationed in Norfolk, and he's made two trips to the Persian Gulf, and he's done very well. He's made a career out of it. He's 10, 11 years in the Navy now, and I know some other young men, too, who are in the military, young women as well, and I think they're doing a great job.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you think the pride for the country and the service and everything is still alive and well?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: That's good. Gentlemen, very good.

sp.speaker: Videographer
sp.p: Did you see any of these concentration camps, Navarria?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Dakow.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Talk a little about it, repeat sort of like --

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: I don't know whether I can talk about it or not.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Why don't you tell us leading up to that. How you got -- how you got there, what we're talking about. Tell me what we're talking about. You were maybe on your way doing battle or after battle or one of the -- how did you find it? How did you --

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Well, it was right towards the end of the war, of course, and we'd been in combat for several days. Without getting -- without getting any rest. And Dakow was not one of our objectives.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Where was that? Where is that located?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: It's south of Munich. It was on our way between -- from Munich to Berchtesgarden. Some other troops had got there first, American troops had got there first. What -- apparently the leaders of our outfit wanted us to see what was there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Well, let me just stop you for a second. Did you even -- did you know about these? How much did the American soldiers even knew about the concentration camps? Was it well known? Was it --

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: I don't remember knowing anything about it. All we knew about was prisoner of war camps. I don't remember knowing anything like this took place. If I did, I had forgotten it. So they put us in trucks and wanted to go and see what was there, and most of the people were -- (Interruption) -- most of the inmates were still there, and the ovens were still warm. There were still remains in the ovens. There were stacks of dead piled feet high all around the outside of the buildings. There were box cars, 40 and 8 box cars with bodies still in them, and the odor was terrible.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: It was just a God-awful sight, that's all, that we just couldn't believe what we saw.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And of course you found out about that all this had been going on?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. And then you wondered what happened? How can this happen? How can human beings do these things to each other?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you think the American troops, if they knew all that when they went over there, would have -- you think it would have been an entirely different attitude? I mean, how do you think that would've -- I mean, that, to me, sounds like it would have changed a few things.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: I think it probably would have, because the outfit that I was in, I don't remember, I don't think, I didn't hear of anything, I don't remember any so-called atrocities where you shot prisoners or that type of thing going on, but I think if we had known that, it might have been different, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You think it was almost like the same thing of them going into Iraq for one reason, for the weapons of mass destruction, and then all of a sudden finding out what's done to all these thousands and thousands and thousands of people and nobody really knew about it until they got over there?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Yeah. It was quite an experience to see that. By that time the combat was over, practically over for us. I have a skull and cross bones I took from an SS trooper, by the way. That's home. We had taken this small town, and the German Warmech were lined up in one part of the town, the town square, waiting for somebody to tell them what to do, and over on the other side of the square was this big, tall, typical Arian, proud SS officer standing all alone. I don't know what he was doing there, because there was no other SS around. And he had a stare. I walked up to him and wanted to get this souvenir off of his jacket lapel, you know, the skull and crossbones. And he looked at me with a steely gaze that would have been a laser shot right through me when I took that off of him. I had my gun, my rifle pointed at him with my finger on the trigger, and I said I'm going to take this skull and crossbones from your lapel, and if you move, you son of a bitch, I'll blow your head off. I don't know whether he understood me or not, but he didn't move. I think he probably understood me, 'cause he looked like he was responding to what I was saying, you know. Okay, I understand. But he never said a word. But these were the characters, I guess, were responsible for the death camps.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What did they do? What did you do with most of the prisoners there? Did they -- did you have a holding place for them or somebody else from another company come in to take them?

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: No. The -- we had troops assigned to the division who were -- would come up after we had taken the town, and take the troops back to the rear area, the Germans back to the rear area. Combat troops, we just -- all we did was stay there until they got there and they would take them.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Videographer
sp.p: If you would be so kind and just look at TJ for a moment, and I'll just take some more pictures just a few sitting quietly.

sp.speaker: Lee P. Riggin
sp.p: Okay.
